claim: The simplest multicellular life cycle is comprised of the growth of the propagule into a colony and its fragmentation to give rise to new propagules.
source: The simplest multicellular life cycle is comprised of the growth of the propagule into a colony and its fragmentation to give rise to new propagules.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about multicellular life cycles presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: The majority of theoretical models assume selection among life cycles to be driven by internal properties of multicellular groups, resulting in growth competition.
source: The majority of theoretical models assume selection among life cycles to be driven by internal properties of multicellular groups, resulting in growth competition.
evidence: This claim characterizes the state of theoretical modeling in the field, drawing on established knowledge of existing models.

claim: The influence of interactions between groups on the evolution of life cycles is rarely even considered.
source: At the same time, the influence of interactions between groups on the evolution of life cycles is rarely even considered.
evidence: This statement characterizes a gap in the literature based on knowledge of existing theoretical approaches.

claim: The outcome of evolution could be coexistence between multiple life cycles when group interactions are considered.
source: Our work shows that the outcome of evolution could be coexistence between multiple life cycles or that the outcome may depend on the initial state of the population – scenarios impossible without group interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model results presented in the manuscript, specifically in sections about competition between life cycles.

claim: The outcome of evolution may depend on the initial state of the population when group interactions are considered.
source: Our work shows that the outcome of evolution could be coexistence between multiple life cycles or that the outcome may depend on the initial state of the population – scenarios impossible without group interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model results showing bistability, as demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: Coexistence between multiple life cycles and initial-state-dependent outcomes are impossible without group interactions.
source: Our work shows that the outcome of evolution could be coexistence between multiple life cycles or that the outcome may depend on the initial state of the population – scenarios impossible without group interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with models without interactions, which always result in a single winner independent of initial conditions.

claim: Evolutionary stable strategies in the model with group interactions are restricted to binary fragmentation.
source: At the same time, we found that some results of these simpler models remain relevant: evolutionary stable strategies in our model are restricted to binary fragmentation – the same class of life cycles that contains all evolutionarily optimal life cycles in the model without interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by analytical results presented in the section 'The set of possible evolutionary stable strategies is restricted'.

claim: Models neglecting interactions can capture short-term dynamics but fall short in predicting the population-scale picture of evolution.
source: Our results demonstrate that while models neglecting interactions can capture short-term dynamics, they fall short in predicting the population-scale picture of evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the model results with and without interactions throughout the manuscript.

claim: Multicellular organisms in all major branches of complex multicellularity are formed by cells staying together after cell division.
source: In all major branches of complex multicellularity (animals, plants, fungi, red and brown algae), organisms are formed by cells staying together after cell division – unlike unicellular species, in which cells part their ways before the next division occurs (Márquez-Zacarías et al., 2021; Herron et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Márquez-Zacarías et al., 2021 and Herron et al., 2022.

claim: In unicellular species, cells part their ways before the next division occurs.
source: In all major branches of complex multicellularity (animals, plants, fungi, red and brown algae), organisms are formed by cells staying together after cell division – unlike unicellular species, in which cells part their ways before the next division occurs (Márquez-Zacarías et al., 2021; Herron et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Márquez-Zacarías et al., 2021 and Herron et al., 2022.

claim: Multicellular organisms must reproduce, otherwise their species will eventually go extinct.
source: However, organisms have to reproduce as otherwise their species will eventually go extinct.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of evolutionary biology based on established knowledge.

claim: For a multicellular organism, reproduction means that some cells must depart in order to develop into an offspring individual.
source: For a multicellular organism, this means that some cells must depart in order to develop into an offspring individual.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of multicellular reproduction.

claim: The combination of organism growth and reproduction constitutes a clonal life cycle.
source: The combination of organism growth and reproduction constitutes a clonal life cycle.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established terminology in the field.

claim: Emergence of clonal multicellular life cycles was the central innovation in the earlier stages of the evolution of multicellularity.
source: Emergence of clonal multicellular life cycles was the central innovation in the earlier stages of the evolution of multicellularity.
evidence: This is a characterization of the importance of life cycles in evolutionary history, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Traits such as the number of cells in the colony, how often cells depart to give rise to new colonies, how large the released propagules are, and how many of them are produced do not exist for unicellular species but become crucial for long-term success of even the most primitive colony of cells.
source: There, traits, which do not even exist for unicellular species, become crucial for long-term success of even the most primitive colony of cells (Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995, Michod, 2007). These include the number of cells in the colony, how often cells depart to give rise to new colonies, how large the released propagules are, and how many of them are produced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995 and Michod, 2007.

claim: The reproduction and fitness of simple cell colonies are dependent on traits such as colony size, cell departure frequency, propagule size, and propagule number.
source: As the reproduction and, consequently, fitness of simple cell colonies are dependent on these traits, they immediately become subjected to natural selection, favoring some life cycles over others.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary theory and the definition of fitness.

claim: Complex multicellular life descends from loose cell colonies.
source: Since complex multicellular life descends from those loose cell colonies, the understanding of the prior evolution of primitive life cycles is essential to our understanding of the later evolution of complex traits (Ratcliff et al., 2012; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; Doulcier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ratcliff et al., 2012; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; Doulcier et al., 2020.

claim: Understanding the prior evolution of primitive life cycles is essential to understanding the later evolution of complex traits.
source: Since complex multicellular life descends from those loose cell colonies, the understanding of the prior evolution of primitive life cycles is essential to our understanding of the later evolution of complex traits (Ratcliff et al., 2012; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; Doulcier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ratcliff et al., 2012; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; Doulcier et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanistically simplest class of models assumes that natural selection operates by means of growth competition.
source: The mechanistically simplest class of models assumes that natural selection operates by means of growth competition.
evidence: This characterizes a class of existing models based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: In growth competition models, colonies are born small, increase in size due to cell divisions, and eventually fragment, so the number of colonies in the population increases.
source: Colonies are born small, but due to cell divisions they increase in size and, eventually, fragment, so the number of colonies in the population increases.
evidence: This describes the basic mechanism of growth competition models based on established knowledge.

claim: The life cycle maximizing the population growth rate has a selective advantage as it outgrows all competitors in growth competition models.
source: The life cycle maximizing the population growth rate has a selective advantage as it outgrows all competitors (Roze and Michod, 2001; Libby et al., 2014; Pichugin et al., 2017; Pichugin et al., 2019; Staps et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020; Gao et al., 2021; Pichugin, 2022; Pichugin and Traulsen, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: For groups made of identical cells, growth competition models predict that only fragmentation into two pieces can evolve if the fragmentation event is instantaneous and costless.
source: For groups made of identical cells, growth competition models of evolution predict that some life cycles cannot be the winners of this growth competition under any conditions. For instance, if the fragmentation event is instantaneous and its execution does not cost anything to the group, only fragmentation into two pieces can evolve (Pichugin et al., 2017; Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pichugin et al., 2017 and Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020.

claim: Division into two pieces is, by a large margin, the most common reproductive strategy among microscopic life forms.
source: And indeed, the division into two pieces is, by a large margin, the most common reproductive strategy among microscopic life forms.
evidence: This is an empirical observation about biological systems based on general knowledge.

claim: Growth competition models assume unconstrained (exponential) growth of the population, which cannot be sustained for a prolonged period of time because resources and space are limited.
source: However, these models, due to their conceptual simplicity, assume unconstrained (exponential) growth of the population, which cannot be sustained for a prolonged period of time, because resources and space are limited.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of exponential growth models based on biological knowledge.

claim: Other models consider density-dependent growth, where the population growth decreases with the number of groups.
source: Other models consider density-dependent growth (Rossetti et al., 2011; Tarnita et al., 2013; van Gestel and Nowak, 2016; Doulcier et al., 2020, Henriques et al., 2021), where the population growth decreases with the number of groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on density-dependent growth models.

claim: The Moran birth–death process on the group level is a similar approach to density-dependent growth, where whenever a new group emerges, one other group dies.
source: A similar approach is the Moran birth–death process on the group level, where whenever a new group emerges, one other group dies (Traulsen and Nowak, 2006; Matias Rodrigues et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2013; Luo, 2014; Kaveh et al., 2016; Olejarz et al., 2018; Cooney, 2019; Cooney, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on Moran processes.

claim: Models with unconstrained and density-dependent growth lead to identical results for life cycle evolution.
source: While the population dynamics of density-dependent population growth is vastly different from the exponential explosion found in models of unconstrained growth, these two approaches lead to identical results for life cycle evolution: as shown in Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020, the dynamics of the fraction of a given life cycle in a population are identical in models with unconstrained and density-dependent growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020.

claim: In models with density-dependent growth, the evolutionary success of the life cycle is still fully determined by the population growth rates.
source: Therefore, even in models with density-dependent growth, the evolutionary success of the life cycle is still fully determined by the population growth rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the equivalence between unconstrained and density-dependent growth models.

claim: Density-dependent growth is a simplification as different groups may differ in their competitiveness.
source: Nevertheless, density-dependent growth is also a simplification as different groups may differ in their competitiveness.
evidence: This is a logical critique of density-dependent models based on biological reasoning.

claim: Large-cell colonies are able to block single cells from access to vital resources.
source: For instance, large-cell colonies are able to block single cells from access to vital resources (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Rainey and Rainey, 2003; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014), which may even lead to a complete extinction of solitary cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Rainey and Rainey, 2003; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014.

claim: Competition between large-cell colonies and single cells may lead to a complete extinction of solitary cells.
source: For instance, large-cell colonies are able to block single cells from access to vital resources (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Rainey and Rainey, 2003; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014), which may even lead to a complete extinction of solitary cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Rainey and Rainey, 2003; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014.

claim: The population dynamics of multicellular life cycles is not necessarily density dependent, but could be frequency dependent.
source: Thus, the population dynamics of multicellular life cycles is not necessarily density dependent, but could be frequency dependent – the impact of resource limitation on the population growth depends on both the size and the composition of the population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different groups differ in competitiveness.

claim: The evolution of multicellular life cycles cannot always be reduced to growth competition, but may arise from eco-evolutionary dynamics.
source: Hence, the evolution of multicellular life cycles cannot always be reduced to growth competition, but may arise from eco-evolutionary dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the argument about frequency-dependent dynamics.

claim: Frequency-dependent dynamics is found to be common among microbial populations.
source: From a broader empirical perspective, frequency-dependent dynamics is found to be common among microbial populations (Levin, 1988; Ribeck and Lenski, 2015; Healey et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levin, 1988; Ribeck and Lenski, 2015; Healey et al., 2016; Friedman et al., 2017.

claim: Frequency-dependent evolutionary dynamics arising from interactions between diverse population members has been considered in detail from the perspective of theoretical ecology.
source: From the perspective of the theoretical ecology, frequency-dependent evolutionary dynamics arising from interactions between diverse population members has also been considered in detail (May, 1972; Wangersky, 1978; Bomze, 1983; Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2017; Bunin, 2017; Barbier et al., 2018; Kotil and Vetsigian, 2018; Tarnita, 2018; Farahpour et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical ecology studies.

claim: The impact of interactions between individuals is recognized in the context of the emergence of aggregative multicellularity.
source: The impact of interactions between individuals is recognized in the context of the emergence of aggregative multicellularity, where cells come together to form collectives (Garcia and De Monte, 2013; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Garcia et al., 2015; Miele and De Monte, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garcia and De Monte, 2013; De Monte and Rainey, 2014; Garcia et al., 2015; Miele and De Monte, 2021.

claim: Both empirical and theoretical ecology approaches tend to overlook frequency dependence in the context of clonal life cycles.
source: However, both empirical and theoretical ecology approaches tend to overlook frequency dependence in the context of clonal life cycles, where the organism's growth in the course of the life cycle may cause a change in its role in interactions (but see an example in Tverskoi and Gavrilets, 2022 modeling evolution of germ–soma differentiation).
evidence: This characterizes a gap in the literature, with a citation to an exception (Tverskoi and Gavrilets, 2022).

claim: Groups die due to both external environmental factors and within-population competition for resources or space.
source: Groups also die due to both external environmental factors and within-population competition for resources or space.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: The fragmentation always occurs by the same pattern and determines the life cycle of a population.
source: The fragmentation always occurs by the same pattern and determines the life cycle of a population.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: In logistic growth, the population approaches the carrying capacity with time, starting from either high or low population size.
source: The characteristic feature of logistic growth is that the population approaches the carrying capacity with time, starting from either high or low populations size (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a known property of logistic growth, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The population dynamics of more complex life cycles bears similarity to the logistic growth of the unicellular life cycle.
source: The population dynamics of more complex life cycles also bears similarity to the logistic growth of the unicellular life cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from the model results.

claim: A composite population containing several subpopulations executing different life cycles reaches a stationary state.
source: A composite population containing several subpopulations executing different life cycles also reaches a stationary state.
evidence: This is an observation from the model results.

claim: The stationary state of a composite population may contain more than one life cycle (coexistence).
source: However, we found that the stationary state may contain more than one life cycle (coexistence).
evidence: This is a finding from the model results.

claim: The stationary state of a composite population may depend on the initial state of the population (multistability).
source: Also, the stationary state may depend on the initial state of the population (multistability).
evidence: This is a finding from the model results.

claim: Coexistence and multistability cannot occur in the linear model without competition.
source: Neither of these can occur in the linear model without competition.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models based on knowledge of their properties.

claim: For a pair of life cycles, there are four possible scenarios of invasion from rare.
source: For a pair of life cycles, there are four possible scenarios of invasion from rare (see the outline in Table 1 and corresponding dynamics in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a classification of possible outcomes presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: When neither life cycle can invade into another, the result is a bistability between life cycles, where the outcome depends on the initial conditions.
source: Finally, the leading eigenvalues of both invasion matrices could be negative – then neither of the life cycles can invade into another. Then, the result is a bistability between life cycles, where the outcome of interactions depends on the initial conditions – another result impossible in the model without competition (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The competition between groups plays a major role in determining which of the four invasion patterns occurs.
source: The competition between groups plays a major role in determining which of the four invasion patterns occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: A life cycle having an advantage in the raw growth rate can be dominated by the result of the competition.
source: For instance, it is possible that a life cycle having an advantage in the raw growth rate (i.e., dominating in the unconstrained growth model) is dominated by the result of the competition (see Figure 3C), where the life cycle 1 + 1 has a faster growth but 2 + 1 still dominates due to the advantage of multicellular groups in competition.
evidence: This is an example from the model results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: About 75% of simulations with multiple life cycles resulted in the survival of a single life cycle across all replicates.
source: The majority of simulations (about 75%) resulted in the survival of a single life cycle across all 100 replicates.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: Coexistence between two or more life cycles was found in about 17% of simulations.
source: The next most common outcome is a coexistence between two or more life cycles – found in about 17% of simulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: Multistability between two or three life cycles was observed in about 6.5% of simulations.
source: Also, a multistability between two or three life cycles was observed in about 6.5% of simulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: More complex outcomes (compositions of multistability and coexistences) contributed to only about 1.5% of simulations.
source: More complex outcomes were also observed – these were the compositions of multistability and coexistences, which contributed to only about 1.5% of simulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: The set of evolutionary stable strategies contains only fragmentations into exactly two pieces.
source: Here, we found that the set of evolutionary stable strategies is similarly restricted – it also contains only fragmentations into exactly two pieces.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical and numerical analysis of the model.

claim: All 64 patterns can be expressed for the same triplet of life cycles for some combination of cell birth, group death, and competition rates.
source: Numerical simulations show that all 64 patterns can be expressed for the same triplet of life cycles for some combination of cell birth, group death, and competition rates (see Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from numerical simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The six most frequent patterns, comprising 77% of the generated dataset, feature a hierarchical dominance.
source: The six most frequent patterns, comprising 77% of the generated dataset, feature a hierarchical dominance, where the life cycles can be ordered in a way that higher-order life cycle dominates (always invade) lower-order life cycles.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: The two most rare patterns feature cyclic dominance, together comprising only 0.015% of the dataset.
source: On the opposite side of the frequency spectrum, the two most rare patterns feature cyclic dominance, together comprising only 0.015% of the dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: In cyclic dominance, in any pair of life cycles one dominates another but the whole triplet follows a 'rock–paper–scissors' dynamics with no evolutionary stable strategies present.
source: There, in any pair of life cycles one dominates another but the whole triplet follows a 'rock–paper–scissors' dynamics with no evolutionary stable strategies present (cf. Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the cyclic dominance pattern with a citation to Park et al., 2020.

claim: Any life cycle with more than two offspring can be constrained.
source: We found that any life cycle with more than two offspring can be constrained (see Appendix 1 for the proof).
evidence: This is a mathematical result proven in Appendix 1.

claim: Only binary fragmentation life cycles can be evolutionary stable strategies.
source: As a result, only binary fragmentation life cycles can be evolutionary stable strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the property that any life cycle with more than two offspring can be constrained.

claim: In a composite population with many life cycles interacting by a victim kernel, only one survives in the long run.
source: We found that in the composite population with many life cycles interacting by a victim kernel, only one survives in the long run (see the proof in Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a mathematical result proven in Appendix 3.

claim: For victim kernels, selection favors the life cycle with the largest carrying capacity.
source: Hence, selection favors the life cycle with the largest carrying capacity because it can grow in a dense population, when all other life cycles die from intense competition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the properties of victim kernels.

claim: In both killer and victim kernels, the evolutionary dynamics is reduced to optimization of a single trait.
source: In both killer and victim kernels, the evolutionary dynamics is reduced to optimization of a single trait: growth rate for the killer kernel and carrying capacity for the victim kernel.
evidence: This is a summary of the results for killer and victim kernels.

claim: The result of selection in killer and victim kernel scenarios is a dominance of a single life cycle over all suboptimal competitors.
source: Thus, the result of selection in these scenarios is a dominance of a single life cycle over all suboptimal competitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of killer and victim kernels.

claim: If a unicellular population is abundant in the system, its stationary state can be explicitly found.
source: If a unicellular population is abundant in the system, its stationary state can be explicitly found (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This is a mathematical result presented in Appendix 4.

claim: The introduction of group competition completely changes the population dynamics of the life cycle growth compared to the model with unconstrained growth.
source: First, the introduction of group competition completely changes the population dynamics of the life cycle growth. Instead of the exponential explosion of the population size occurring in the model with unconstrained population size, the growth in our current model slows down with the population size.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and previous models.

claim: In the model with group competition, the population approaches a stationary state with limited population size and constant composition.
source: Eventually, the population approaches a stationary state with the limited population size and constant composition (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Evolution in the model with unconstrained growth always results in a survival of a single life cycle, independently of the initial conditions.
source: By contrast, evolution in the model with unconstrained growth always results in a survival of a single life cycle, independently of the initial conditions.
evidence: This is a known property of models with unconstrained growth based on previous work.

claim: The restrictions on the possible evolutionary stable strategies are exactly the same in the models with and without population size constraints.
source: Third, despite all the differences in the population and evolutionary dynamics, the restrictions on the possible evolutionary stable strategies are exactly the same in the models with and without population size constraints (see section 'The set of possible evolutionary stable strategies is restricted').
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and previous models.

claim: In both models with and without population size constraints, an ESS may only feature a fragmentation into exactly two pieces.
source: In both models, an ESS may only feature a fragmentation into exactly two pieces.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of both models.

claim: Any life cycle producing more than two offspring can always be invaded by another life cycle with a smaller number of offspring.
source: Any life cycle producing more than two offspring can always be invaded by another life cycle with a smaller number of offspring.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claim: Life cycles with fragmentation into multiple pieces may become evolutionary stable strategies if fragmentation is costly.
source: Beyond the scope of our model, life cycles with fragmentation into multiple pieces may become evolutionary stable strategies if fragmentation is costly (e.g., imposes a risk of cell loss).
evidence: This is a speculation about extensions of the model.

claim: Under a costly fragmentation scenario, binary fragmentation is no longer special as a fragmentation into multiple pieces can win growth rate competition.
source: There, binary fragmentation is no longer special as a fragmentation into multiple pieces can win growth rate competition.
evidence: This is a speculation about the behavior of models with costly fragmentation.

claim: Constrained triplets of life cycles still exist under a costly fragmentation scenario but the constraining condition is different.
source: Nevertheless, constrained triplets of life cycles still exist under a costly fragmentation scenario but the constraining condition is different from the one presented here. There, a life cycle containing two different subsets of offspring with the same combined size is constrained between two life cycles, which use either of these subsets twice (Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pichugin and Traulsen, 2020.

claim: The dynamical equations in the present model bear a similarity with the generalized Lotka–Volterra (GLV) equations.
source: In the broad context of the eco-evolutionary dynamics, our dynamical Equations (2) and (7) bear a similarity with the generalized Lotka–Volterra (GLV) equations widely used in ecology: both contain a linear growth term and a nonlinear competition term (typically of the second order) balancing out the linear growth.
evidence: This is a comparison between the model and GLV equations.

claim: The equations in the present model are not equivalent to the GLV equations.
source: However, our equations are not equivalent to the GLV.
evidence: This is a clarification about the relationship between the model and GLV equations.

claim: Competition plays a major role in the evolution of multicellular life cycles.
source: In this article, we found that the competition plays a major role in the evolution of multicellular life cycles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The demographics of simple multicellular species is not sufficiently studied experimentally.
source: Unfortunately, the demographics of simple multicellular species is not sufficiently studied experimentally.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of empirical research.

claim: In Pseudomonas fluorescens, initially unicellular bacteria evolve 'glue' production, which causes formation of multicellular aggregates.
source: In a still liquid media, these initially unicellular bacteria evolve a 'glue' production, which causes formation of multicellular aggregates.
evidence: This is an empirical observation about P. fluorescens.

claim: Pseudomonas fluorescens aggregates float atop the media, gaining an exclusive access to oxygen.
source: These aggregates float atop the media, gaining an exclusive access to oxygen.
evidence: This is an empirical observation about P. fluorescens aggregates.

claim: Once the entire surface is covered by continuous bacterial biofilm in P. fluorescens cultures, the unicellular phenotype living in the body of the media is completely denied the oxygen access and dies out.
source: Once the entire surface is covered by continuous bacterial biofilm, the unicellular phenotype living in the body of the media is completely denied the oxygen access and dies out.
evidence: This is an empirical observation about P. fluorescens population dynamics.

claim: In the P. fluorescens system, the more cells there are in the group, the more stress they apply to others and the more resistant to competition they are.
source: Naturally, the more cells there are in the group, the more stress they apply to others and, at the same time, the more resistant to competition they are.
evidence: This is an inference about competition dynamics in P. fluorescens based on biological reasoning.

claim: Figure 1B shows that group growth and fragmentation together constitute a life cycle, in which initially small groups grow in size and eventually fragment, giving rise to more small groups.
source: (B) Together, group growth and fragmentation constitute a life cycle, in which initially small groups grow in size and eventually fragment, giving rise to more small groups.
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 1B.

claim: Figure 2B and C show that for multicellular life cycles, the population approaches a stationary state from any initial state.
source: (B, C) For multicellular life cycles (2 + 1 depicted), the population also approaches such a stationary state from any initial state.
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 2B and C.

claim: Figure 3 shows that competitive interactions in a pair of life cycles can lead to bistability, dominance of either life cycle, or coexistence.
source: Each panel shows the evolutionary trajectories of populations with various initial abundances of the life cycles 1 + 1 and 2 + 1 (lines) and all final states (dots).
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 3.

claim: Figure 4B shows that about 75% of simulations resulted in a single life cycle, about 17% in coexistence, about 6.5% in multistability, and about 1.5% in other configurations.
source: (B) The frequencies of various classes of outcomes. A single life cycle (yellow) is the most common. Coexistence of life cycles (red) and bistability between them (blue) are less common. More complex composite configurations (gray) are also possible, but found rarely.
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 4B.

claim: Figure 6 shows four patterns of evolutionary dynamics in constrained triplets: hierarchical dominance, bistability, coexistence, and non-hierarchical dominance.
source: Four patterns are shown here and four more are symmetric to them. Blue lines are population dynamics trajectories with different initial composition of the population. Red points are final states. Black arrows show directions of invasion from rare.
evidence: This describes the content of Figure 6.

claim: In constrained triplets, hierarchical dominance was observed in about 78% of entries.
source: In a larger dataset (66,000 entries) with random birth, death, and competition rates, hierarchical dominance was observed in about 78% of entries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: In constrained triplets, coexistence between all three life cycles is observed in 11% of the dataset.
source: Two more patterns feature a coexistence between all three life cycles (see Figure 6C). Note that unlike a pair of life cycles with unique coexistence equilibrium considered in section 'Competition between pairs of life cycles may result in coexistence or bistability,' the triplet features a range of stable coexistence states. The coexistence pattern is similarly frequent, observed in 11% of the dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.

claim: In constrained triplets, non-hierarchical dominance patterns appear with frequency smaller than 0.01% of cases.
source: Finally, the least frequent two patterns are non-hierarchical dominance, where one constraining life cycle dominates another, but in the abundance of the constrained life cycle, the invasion pattern is inverse (see Figure 6D). They appear with three orders of magnitude lower frequency, smaller than 0.01% of cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from numerical simulations.
